title: Bar Charts and Histograms
summary: Learn to compare categories with plt.bar() and reveal distributions with plt.hist(), understanding the zero-baseline rule and the bins parameter.

steps.title: Comparing Cities with a Bar Chart
steps.lede: When you want to compare a number across discrete categories, a bar chart aligns every bar to a shared baseline so the eye can judge lengths at a glance.

blocks.text: Suppose you want to compare average delivery time across Lagos, Abuja, and Kano. A bar chart is a common chart type for graphing categorical data or data sorted into groups — which fits this comparison exactly.

`plt.bar(x, height)` (or `ax.bar(x, height)`) makes a bar plot with bars positioned at the given x coordinates and given heights, with the baseline defaulting to 0. Categorical names can be passed directly as the x argument: `plt.bar(city_avg.index, city_avg)` plots the three city names as bar positions and each city's average delivery time as the bar height.

steps.title: Why the Baseline Must Start at Zero
steps.lede: The bar chart's power comes from comparing lengths — and that only works when every bar starts at the same point.

blocks.text: Bar charts are easy to interpret because the eye is good at comparing lengths when the objects being compared are aligned to a common baseline. Every bar starts at 0, so a taller bar genuinely represents a larger value — Kano's bar looks taller than Lagos's because its average delivery time is higher.

Starting bars at a value other than 0 — say 20 minutes — distorts the comparison. If Kano averages 30 minutes and Lagos 25, bars starting at 20 are 10 and 5 units tall: Kano's bar looks twice as long even though its average is only 5 minutes higher. Keep the baseline at 0.

steps.title: When to Use a Bar Chart
steps.lede: Which kind of data is a bar chart designed to compare?

public.prompt: Which of the following datasets is a bar chart the right tool to visualise?

options.text: Average delivery time for each of three cities (Lagos, Abuja, Kano)
Daily average delivery time over five consecutive days
The distribution of individual delivery times across all orders
The relationship between delivery distance and delivery time

opt_city.message: Correct. A bar chart is a common chart type for graphing categorical data or data sorted into groups — here, the three cities are the categories and the bar heights show each city's average.

opt_time.message: Not quite. Daily averages over consecutive days form an ordered time series — a line plot is better suited to show how the value changes over time.

opt_dist.message: Not quite. Showing the distribution of a numeric variable across many values is what a histogram does — it bins the values and draws one bar per bin.

opt_rel.message: Not quite. Exploring the relationship between two numeric variables is what a scatter plot does — it places one point per (x, y) pair.

correct.message: Right. A bar chart is designed for categorical data — comparing a numeric value across discrete groups such as cities.

incorrect.message: A bar chart is a common chart type for graphing categorical data or data sorted into groups. The three cities are categories, so a bar chart is the right choice for comparing their averages.

hints: Think about which dataset has discrete, named groups rather than a continuous numeric axis.
A bar chart compares a numeric value across categories — which option has categories?

steps.title: The Zero-Baseline Rule
steps.lede: Why must a bar chart's baseline start at zero?

public.prompt: Kano averages 30 minutes and Lagos averages 25 minutes. A bar chart is drawn with the baseline starting at 20 minutes instead of 0. What is wrong with this chart?

options.text: Kano's bar looks twice as long as Lagos's even though its average is only 5 minutes higher
Nothing — starting at 20 makes the difference between cities easier to see
The chart is missing a title, which makes it unreadable
Bar charts cannot display averages — only counts

opt_distort.message: Correct. With a baseline at 20, Kano's bar is 10 units tall and Lagos's is 5 units tall — Kano looks twice as long even though its average is only 5 minutes higher. The eye compares bar lengths from the baseline, so the baseline must be 0.

opt_fine.message: Not quite. Starting at a non-zero baseline distorts the comparison. Bar charts are easy to read because the eye compares lengths from a common baseline — if that baseline is not 0, the lengths no longer truthfully represent the values.

opt_missing.message: Not quite. A missing title is a labeling issue, not a baseline issue. The real problem is that starting bars at 20 instead of 0 makes Kano's bar look twice as long as Lagos's, distorting the comparison.

opt_wrong_type.message: Not quite. Bar charts can display any numeric value per category, including averages. The problem here is the non-zero baseline, which distorts the visual comparison of bar lengths.

correct.message: Exactly. A non-zero baseline makes bar lengths misleading — Kano's bar looks twice as long as Lagos's even though the difference is only 5 minutes. Keep the baseline at 0.

incorrect.message: Bar charts are easy to read because the eye compares lengths from a common baseline. If the baseline is not 0, the lengths distort the comparison. With a baseline at 20, Kano's bar (10 units) looks twice as long as Lagos's (5 units) even though the difference is only 5 minutes.

hints: Calculate the bar heights when the baseline is 20: Kano = 30 − 20 = ?, Lagos = 25 − 20 = ?
The eye compares bar *lengths* from the baseline — what happens to those lengths when the baseline shifts?

steps.title: Seeing the Distribution with a Histogram
steps.lede: A histogram bins a numeric variable and draws one bar per bin — revealing the shape of the distribution rather than individual values.

blocks.text: A bar chart compares categories, but delivery times are a numeric variable. You might instead want to see how those times are distributed — how many deliveries were fast, how many were slow, and whether most cluster in the middle. A histogram answers that question.

`plt.hist(x, bins=...)` uses `numpy.histogram` to bin the data in x, count the number of values in each bin, and draw the result as bars. `plt.hist(orders['delivery_time_minutes'])` bins every delivery time and shows how many orders fall into each time range.

The `bins` parameter defaults to `rcParams['hist.bins']`, which defaults to 10. Passing an integer sets that many equal-width bins; passing a sequence sets explicit bin edges; passing a string such as `'auto'` selects a binning strategy automatically.

before.code:
# Delivery times as a sorted list — shape is not visible
print(sorted(orders['delivery_time_minutes'].tolist()))

annotations.text: A sorted list shows individual values but not the distribution shape
plt.hist bins the values and draws one bar per bin, revealing the distribution shape

blocks.change_summary: plt.hist() replaces a sorted list with a binned bar chart that reveals the distribution shape.

segments.label: plt.hist() with a bin count and with explicit bin edges
segments.summary: Starting from the observation that plotting one bar per age would produce nearly a hundred columns, the presenter introduces histograms as a way to group values into bins. plt.hist() is called on a list of ages with bins=5, producing five equal-width bars whose heights show how many ages fall in each range. An edgecolor argument is added to make individual bins distinguishable. The presenter then replaces the integer with an explicit list [10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60], showing that six edge values produce five bins with exact decade boundaries, and reads the per-bin counts aloud.

steps.title: How plt.hist() Works
steps.lede: What does plt.hist() do with the values you pass it?

public.prompt: What does `plt.hist(orders['delivery_time_minutes'])` do internally before drawing the bars?

options.text: Uses numpy.histogram to bin the values and count how many fall in each bin
Sorts the delivery times and draws one bar per unique value
Computes the average delivery time and draws a single bar
Places one point per delivery time along the x-axis

opt_bin.message: Correct. `plt.hist()` uses `numpy.histogram` to bin the data in x, count the number of values in each bin, and draw the result as bars — one bar per bin.

opt_sort.message: Not quite. `plt.hist()` groups values into bins (ranges), not one bar per unique value. Drawing one bar per unique value would produce too many bars for continuous data.

opt_avg.message: Not quite. `plt.hist()` shows the distribution of all values, not a single summary. It bins the data and draws one bar per bin, showing how many values fall in each range.

opt_scatter.message: Not quite. Placing one point per value is what a scatter plot does. `plt.hist()` groups values into bins and draws one bar per bin, showing the count in each range.

correct.message: Right. `plt.hist()` uses `numpy.histogram` to bin the data and count values per bin, then draws one bar per bin — revealing the distribution shape.

incorrect.message: `plt.hist(x, bins=...)` uses `numpy.histogram` to bin the data in x, count the number of values in each bin, and draw the result as bars.

hints: The fact says `plt.hist()` uses a specific numpy function — which one?
Think about what 'binning' means: grouping values into ranges and counting how many fall in each.

steps.title: Controlling Bin Count
steps.lede: What does passing an integer to the bins parameter do?

public.prompt: Which of the following is a valid way to call `plt.hist()` that sets explicit bin edges at 10, 20, 30, 40, and 50 minutes?

opt_seq.message: Correct. Passing a sequence sets explicit bin edges — here the four bins are [10, 20), [20, 30), [30, 40), and [40, 50], exactly as specified.

opt_int.message: Not quite. Passing an integer sets that many *equal-width* bins — the edges are computed automatically from the data range, not set explicitly. To set explicit edges, pass a sequence.

opt_auto.message: Not quite. Passing the string `'auto'` selects a binning strategy automatically — the edges are chosen by the algorithm, not set explicitly. To set explicit edges, pass a sequence.

opt_default.message: Not quite. Calling `plt.hist()` without a `bins` argument uses the default of 10 equal-width bins. To set explicit bin edges, pass a sequence such as `[10, 20, 30, 40, 50]`.

correct.message: Exactly. Passing a sequence to `bins` sets explicit bin edges — the four bins are [10, 20), [20, 30), [30, 40), and [40, 50].

incorrect.message: The `bins` parameter accepts three forms: an integer (equal-width bins), a sequence (explicit edges), or a string strategy such as `'auto'`. To set explicit edges at 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, pass a list.

hints: The question asks for *explicit* bin edges — which form of `bins` sets the edges directly?
An integer sets the *number* of bins; a sequence sets the *edges*.

steps.title: Bar Charts and Histograms: What You Learned
steps.lede: Two chart types, two different questions — categories versus distribution.

blocks.text: Use `plt.bar(x, height)` to compare a numeric value across discrete categories, keeping the baseline at 0 so bar lengths stay honest. Use `plt.hist(x, bins=...)` to reveal how a numeric variable is distributed — it bins the values and draws one bar per bin.

remediation_steps.title: Bar Charts Are for Categories
remediation_steps.lede: A bar chart compares a numeric value across discrete groups — not distributions or trends.

blocks.text: A bar chart is a common chart type for graphing categorical data or data sorted into groups. The three cities Lagos, Abuja, and Kano are discrete categories, so a bar chart comparing their average delivery times is the right fit. A histogram would show the spread of times, not a city-by-city comparison.

remediation_steps.title: The Baseline Must Be Zero
remediation_steps.lede: Shifting the baseline away from zero makes bars misleading because the eye compares lengths.

blocks.text: Bar charts are easy to interpret because the eye compares lengths from a common baseline. If Kano averages 30 minutes and Lagos 25, bars starting at 20 are 10 and 5 units tall — Kano's bar looks twice as long even though its average is only 5 minutes higher. Keep the baseline at 0 so lengths stay proportional to values.

remediation_steps.title: How plt.hist() Bins Your Data
remediation_steps.lede: plt.hist() doesn't just count values — it groups them into bins first.

blocks.text: `plt.hist(x, bins=...)` uses `numpy.histogram` to bin the data in x, count the number of values in each bin, and draw the result as bars. Each bar represents a range of values, not a single value — that's what makes a histogram different from a bar chart.

remediation_steps.title: Controlling Bins in plt.hist()
remediation_steps.lede: The bins parameter accepts an integer, a sequence, or a strategy string.

blocks.text: The `bins` parameter defaults to `rcParams['hist.bins']`, which defaults to 10. Passing an integer sets that many equal-width bins. Passing a sequence sets explicit bin edges. Passing a string such as `'auto'` selects a binning strategy automatically.
